tools.name: aide_discover
tools.description:
Scan for .aide spec files in this project. Returns a tree map of where specs live, following progressive disclosure.

Without a path: returns a lightweight project-wide map — file locations, type tags and each spec's one-line description; a plan or todo tag carries its status, e.g. [plan: approved]. Only the head of each file is read. Use this once to understand the project's spec architecture.

With a path: the response opens with the ancestor chain — the cascading intent lineage from project root down to the target directory, with each ancestor showing its description and alignment status (aligned/misaligned when set). The ancestor chain gives you the full inherited context before you read a single spec body. After the ancestor chain comes the detailed subtree of the target directory — summaries extracted from file content and anomaly warnings. Use this to drill into the area you're working on.

.aide files are progressive disclosure specs that live next to orchestrator code — they contain intent (strategy, implementation contracts, anti-patterns), research (sources, data, patterns), or QA checklists (todo). Read .aide files BEFORE reading code — they are the context layer between folder structure and implementation details.

File types (.aide, intent.aide, research.aide, plan.aide, todo.aide):
- .aide — Intent spec (default). Strategy, contracts, anti-patterns.
- intent.aide — Same as .aide, used only when research.aide exists in the same folder.
- research.aide — Raw research. Sources, data points, pattern synthesis.
- plan.aide -- Architect's implementation plan. Checkboxed steps for the implementor.
- todo.aide — QA re-alignment document. Captures where implementation drifted from intent.

Never have both .aide and intent.aide in the same folder.

path.description: Subdirectory to drill into. When provided, the response opens with the ancestor chain — the cascading intent lineage from root to target, each ancestor showing its description and alignment status — followed by the detailed subtree with summaries and warnings. When omitted, returns a shallow project-wide map (locations, type tags with plan/todo status, and spec descriptions).

tools.name: aide_read
tools.description: Read an .aide spec file with full context. Returns the file content, its classified type (intent/research/plan/todo), related specs in the same directory, and links found in the content (relative paths, inline references, URLs). Use this after aide_discover to drill into a specific spec.

path.description: Path to the .aide file to read

tools.name: aide_scaffold
tools.description:
Create a new AIDE working file from its blank template, under its canonical name. It never overwrites: a request for a file that already exists, filled or empty, is a no-op reported as a skip line — remove a file first with aide_cleanup to replace it. New files start with their starting value: an intent spec alignment: unreviewed, a plan or todo list status: proposed. Handles the naming rules, so never pick a name yourself: in a module folder, intent specs are .aide by default, but become intent.aide when research.aide exists in the same folder. Creating a research.aide auto-renames any existing .aide to intent.aide. The project root intent spec always lands at .aide/intent.aide: pass directory ".aide" or "." (both mean the project's .aide folder for intent, research and both). A bare .aide/.aide left by an older project, with no intent.aide beside it, is renamed to .aide/intent.aide with its content kept; if .aide/intent.aide exists, nothing changes. Folders are never treated as spec files. A plan needs an intent spec beside it: scaffolding a plan in a folder with no intent spec (.aide or intent.aide; a research.aide alone does not count) is refused and creates nothing — write the folder's intent spec first. For a root-level plan, pass directory ".aide".

Types:
- intent — Strategy, contracts, anti-patterns
- research — Sources, data, patterns (triggers rename of existing .aide)
- both — Creates research.aide + intent.aide pair
- todo — QA re-alignment document for QA agents
- plan — Architect's implementation plan; refused unless the folder already holds an intent spec
- session — The project's session record, always at .aide/session.aide whatever directory you pass: the empty placeholder with every section heading. Its single source; never write the placeholder by hand.

directory.description: Directory where the .aide file(s) will be created. For the project root intent spec pass ".aide" or "."; it lands at .aide/intent.aide

type.description: Type of file to create: intent, research, both, todo, plan, or session (always .aide/session.aide)

tools.name: aide_cleanup
tools.description:
Remove a module's pipeline ephemerals (plan.aide, todo.aide, brief.aide) once that module's cycle has closed, leaving the code and the intent specs as the durable record. It never removes, rewrites or reads anything else: intent specs, research specs, code, and .aide/session.aide are all out of reach.

Each file it would remove must record a closed status: completed (re-checked — every checkbox really checked) or abandoned. A file from before statuses existed, with no status but every checkbox checked, also passes. It refuses anything still proposed or approved, a completed file with an open item, a brief.aide with no plan.aide beside it, and a folder with no ephemerals. An abandoned plan takes its brief with it, and where there is no plan.aide a closed todo.aide is removed on its own. A refusal names each open file or item with its file and line, and nothing is removed. Record a closing status with aide_frontmatter first; this tool never sets or infers one.

Call it directly, because the real call is already safe. dryRun is an optional preview for inspection only and is never a required step before the real call.

This is the cross-platform replacement for a shell delete, so it can be permitted by name.

path.description: The module directory whose ephemerals to remove, relative to the project root

dryRun.description: Optional. Removes nothing and only reports what a real call would remove. Agents closing a module omit it.

tools.name: aide_frontmatter
tools.description: Read or change one governed frontmatter value of an AIDE file, leaving every other byte untouched. Intent specs carry alignment (unreviewed, aligned, misaligned). plan.aide, brief.aide and todo.aide carry one status lifecycle: proposed, approved, completed, abandoned. Only allowed moves are accepted, completed is refused while any item is unchecked or, for a brief, until its plan is completed, and a refusal names the allowed next values. Call with path alone to read a file's governed value without changing it. The session record, research specs and brain.aide carry no governed values. The tool never chooses a value; the caller decides.

path.description: Path of the AIDE file, relative to the project root

field.description: Governed field to change: alignment (intent specs) or status (plans, todo lists, briefs). Omit with value to read.

value.description: New value for field. Omit with field to read.

tools.name: aide_validate
tools.description: Health check for .aide spec files in the project. Detects orphaned specs (a spec whose folder, subfolders included, holds no code — only AIDE files, Markdown and dot-files; the project root intent spec in .aide/ is never orphaned, and a plan's presence never decides it), plans with no intent spec beside them (plan-without-spec — write the folder's spec, never delete the plan), missing specs (orchestrators with 3+ helper imports but no .aide), naming conflicts (.aide + intent.aide in same folder), broken links, orphaned research (research.aide without intent spec), missing descriptions (specs with no description field in frontmatter), files whose frontmatter cannot be parsed, and intent specs whose alignment is missing (missing-alignment) or not one of unreviewed, aligned, misaligned (invalid-alignment).

path.description: Subdirectory to validate (defaults to entire project)

tools.name: aide_upgrade
tools.description:
Compare the AIDE methodology artifacts in this project against the canonical versions and return structured JSON results grouped by category. Use this when the user asks to update AIDE, sync AIDE, refresh AIDE, check for AIDE updates, or bring AIDE up to date. This is NOT for editing user .aide specs — it inspects methodology infrastructure only.

The tool uses a two-call pattern for progressive disclosure:

**First call (no `category` param):** Returns a lightweight summary — every category with file names, statuses, and counts, but NO file content. Use this to understand what has drifted and present a summary to the user. Ask which categories they want to apply.

**Second call (with `category` param):** The tool writes all differs/missing files directly to disk itself and returns a manifest — file results with `filePath`, `status` (`"updated"`, `"created"`, or `"unchanged"`), and `name`, but NO `canonicalContent`. The agent never sees file content and never uses the Write tool for methodology files.

Repeat the second call for each category the user confirms.

As the calling agent, you must:
1. Call without `category` first to get the summary
2. Present each drifted category (differs/missing) and ask the user which to apply
3. For each confirmed category, call again with `category=X` — the tool writes the files and returns a manifest. Report what was updated/created to the user.
4. For the `mcp` category, a result that carries `prescription` is merged into the existing MCP config by you (read → merge → write). A result that carries `pinMove` or `globalSwitch` is never merged by hand: the tool writes it (see the MCP step). If `malformed`, tell the user — do not overwrite.
5. For `ide`, the manifest may include `instructions` for VS Code extension install — execute that command for the user. Zed config is written directly by the tool.
6. For `brain`, the summary reports `missingSections`, outdated section text as `staleSections` and a legacy brain launcher as `legacyLauncher` (its reasons), each named separately. The brain category then works through three calls, each one decision at a time:
   a. `category: "brain"` (after the user's yes) inserts every missing section from the latest bundled template — byte-identical, in the file's line endings — only when the config launches the template's own brain server. It returns `{ outcome: "inserted", inserted }` (markers only; empty when nothing is missing) or `{ outcome: "adapt", adapt, instructions }` naming the sections the user must write for their backend.
   b. `category: "brain"` with `brainChange: <marker | "launcher">` returns one `{ outcome: "change", target, before, after, beforeHash }` diff to show the user. It is read-only. For a non-template config it returns `missing` with the template's version of an absent section instead.
   c. The same call plus that `beforeHash`, only on the user's yes to that one diff, returns `applied`, or a `refused` re-fetch instruction when the bytes changed since the preview.
   Never batch changes under one yes. Every refusal's `instructions` names the next step.

**IMPORTANT — one-at-a-time wizard pattern using AskUserQuestion:**
Do NOT present all categories at once. Walk the user through ONE category at a time using AskUserQuestion with Yes/Skip options. Stop after each question and wait for confirmation before calling with that category.

Categories: pointer-stub, methodology-docs, version-metadata, commands, agents, skills, mcp, ide, readme, brain.

Upgrade surface (user code and user .aide specs are never touched):
- AIDE pointer stub in the agent config file
- Canonical methodology docs under .aide/docs/
- versions.json metadata under .aide/docs/
- Slash commands for all pipeline phases
- Pipeline agent files, skill templates
- MCP server entry in the project's MCP config
- IDE file association config (Zed settings, VS Code extension)
- The user-owned brain config, only through the brain category: missing sections and confirmed migrations, one consented change at a time

Supports Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and Copilot. Auto-detects the framework or accepts an override.

**MCP step:** the canonical aide entry runs the global command `aidemd-mcp`. The entry is read under the `aide` key, or under `aidemd-mcp` when there is no `aide` key; the key is never renamed. Without `targetVersion`, an entry that launches through npx reports `differs` with `globalSwitch: { key, name, installed, installCommand }` and no prescription. Tell the user npx launches time out at session start and ask; on yes, run `installCommand` via Bash first unless `installed` is true (a failed install: say so and stop). Then `category: "mcp"` makes the tool rewrite only that entry's command and args to the global command, every other byte unchanged; it re-checks the global install and, while the package is missing, keeps `differs` and returns `instructions` naming the install command — install, then call again. A missing aide entry returns the global `prescription` plus `globalPackage`; when the package is not installed it also carries `instructions` — act on them: install first, then merge, and never merge after a failed install. An older server cannot switch itself, so a pinned project first moves its pin to a newer version with `targetVersion` (only under the `aide` key; an npx entry under `aidemd-mcp` gets `instructions` to call without `targetVersion` and switch instead) — an exact published `x.y.z`, normally `aide_info`'s `behind.latest`, valid only with no category or with `category: "mcp"`. With it, a local (npx) aide entry is judged by its version pin alone: an older, missing or non-exact pin reports `differs` with `pinMove: { from, to }` (`from` is null when unpinned) and no prescription; a pin at or ahead of the target `matches` and is never moved back. Install the target first (`npx -y @aidemd-mcp/server@{to} sync --help` prints help starting `Usage:` and exits 2 by design; anything else means the install failed — then stop and move nothing). Then `category: "mcp"` with the same `targetVersion` makes the tool write the move itself, changing only the version inside the package argument — the command form, `cmd /c`, `-y`, other servers, formatting and line endings stay byte-identical — and returns `status: "updated"` with `pinMove`. A result that keeps `status: "differs"` with `instructions` means nothing was written (the pin changed since it was checked, the config cannot be edited byte-safely, or the entry is not a locatable `@aidemd-mcp/server` spec): relay the instructions. A global entry is never moved; the target is ignored for it. A moved pin takes effect only in a new session — tell the user to start one. An `aidemd-mcp` entry matches as the bare command or an absolute-path shim of it; a path-launched one may carry `tip`, an informational remark to mention once — never drift, never a merge question. Any other (custom) command under the `aide` key is left alone and reports `matches`. The brain entry is not part of the `mcp` step; a legacy brain launcher is changed only through the brain category's `brainChange: "launcher"` preview and apply, on the user's yes.

framework.description: Force a specific framework instead of auto-detecting. Auto-detection checks for framework-specific files/directories and defaults to Claude Code.

path.description: Custom project root path (defaults to server working directory)

category.description: When provided, applies that category. For package-owned categories the call writes all differs/missing files to disk and returns a manifest (no canonicalContent). For `brain` it inserts missing sections (no `brainChange`), previews one change (`brainChange` alone), or applies it (`brainChange` + `beforeHash`); it never rewrites an existing section outside an applied change. When omitted, return all categories as metadata-only summaries (no canonicalContent fields).

brainChange.description: Brain-category-only selector for one stale section (its marker) or the legacy launcher (`launcher`). Without `beforeHash` the call previews that one change read-only; with `beforeHash` it applies it.

beforeHash.description: The `beforeHash` a `brainChange` preview returned. Turns the call into the guarded apply: the change is written only if the current bytes still hash to this value.

targetVersion.description: Exact published x.y.z version to judge the project's local aide entry's npx pin against (normally aide_info's behind.latest). With category "mcp" the tool moves the pin to it, changing only the version; with no category the move is shown read-only as pinMove. Not valid with any other category. A global entry is never moved.

tools.name: aide_info
tools.description:
Boot-time reporter called by the orchestrator at startup. Returns independent top-level fields that the orchestrator must branch on separately:

**`outdated` (array of stale artifact keys) — soft notification.**
Compares the host's `.aide/versions.json` against the canonical manifest shipped with this running server — never against the latest published version, so files that match the version the project runs are current even when a newer release exists. Each element names an artifact key that is behind. An empty array means everything is current. A missing `.aide/versions.json` (old install predating version tracking) silently collapses to `[]`. Staleness is informational — the orchestrator continues with a heads-up to the user.

**`behind` (`{ installed, latest, launch, versionsBehind, highlights }` or null) — soft notification.** Non-null when the running server is older than the latest published version, whatever launch the project's `aide` entry uses — a global install or npx, pinned or not. `installed` is the running server's version. `launch` (`global` or `local`) picks the remedy: `global` → `npm i -g @aidemd-mcp/server@{latest}`; `local` → first install `latest` into the npx cache, then move the project's aide pin to it with `aide_upgrade({ category: "mcp", targetVersion: latest })`, never a hand edit of `.mcp.json`; if the install fails, switch nothing; once the newer server runs, `/aide:upgrade` offers to switch the entry to the global command. `versionsBehind` (1 or more) counts the published releases after `installed` up to `latest`; `highlights` holds 0–3 one-line notes of what they added or fixed (empty when the release notes were unavailable). Show the count and highlights briefly, never the changelog. Either upgrade takes effect only in a new session. It never gates the pipeline. Null when there is no `aide` entry, the running version is unknown, the server is current, or the version check could not run (offline checks pass silently).

**`brainMigration` (`{ staleSections, legacyLauncher }` or null) — soft notification.** Non-null when the brain config has sections whose text matches an earlier template version, or a legacy brain launcher (`legacyLauncher` lists the reasons: npx-launch, unpinned, unversioned, older-pin, missing-auto-confirm). Mention it once and suggest `/aide:brain config`; it never gates the pipeline and never changes `brain.status`.

**`brain` (precondition state) — hard gate.**
Reports whether the host's brain MCP entry is wired and consistent. Shape: `{ status, name?, fault?, hints }` — `name` is absent on `no-brain-aide` and `brain-aide-invalid`; `fault` is present only on `brain-aide-invalid`. The orchestrator must halt and direct the user to resolve the issue before continuing if `status` is not `'ok'`. No path validation is performed — the package never stats any directory on disk; state derives entirely from comparing `.aide/config/brain.aide` against `.mcp.json`.

The five `brain.status` values:
- `ok` — `.aide/config/brain.aide` exists, satisfies the required-section contract, and the host's `.mcp.json` `brain` entry matches the parsed `mcpServerConfig`. `name` is the user-declared descriptive label from brain.aide. The pipeline may proceed.
- `no-brain-aide` — `.aide/config/brain.aide` is absent. No `name` field. Remediation: run `/aide:brain config`, which creates the config.
- `brain-aide-invalid` — the file exists but falls short. `fault.kind` is `missing-sections` (with `fault.sections` naming each missing required section) or `malformed` (with `fault.reason`). No `name` field. Remediation: run `/aide:brain config`.
- `no-mcp-entry` — brain.aide parsed successfully but the host's `.mcp.json` is absent, malformed, or has no `mcpServers.brain` key. `name` is present. Remediation: run sync with the same launcher the project's `aide` MCP entry uses — `aidemd-mcp sync` when the project's `aide` MCP entry runs the globally installed `aidemd-mcp`, or `npx -y @aidemd-mcp/server@<version> sync` with the version that entry pins when it runs through npx.
- `mcp-drift` — brain.aide and `.mcp.json` both exist but their `brain` entries disagree on `command` or `args`. `name` is present. Remediation: run sync with the same launcher the project's `aide` MCP entry uses — `aidemd-mcp sync` when the project's `aide` MCP entry runs the globally installed `aidemd-mcp`, or `npx -y @aidemd-mcp/server@<version> sync` with the version that entry pins when it runs through npx.

`hints` is always present on every status — an array of candidate brain root paths the orchestrator can surface during recovery.

No parameters needed — uses the server's working directory.

tools.name: aide_brain
tools.description:
On-demand brain entry-point tool. Call this when you need to reach the brain mid-task — do NOT call it on every /aide boot. Boot-time brain precondition state is already reported by aide_info.brain.status; firing aide_brain at boot duplicates that work unnecessarily. It is also how a brain config is set up, repaired or written for any backend, one decision at a time. Every mode is read-only: no call writes to disk.

**Optional `source` parameter** — which read runs. Omitted means `"host"`.
- `"host"` — one section of the host's `.aide/config/brain.aide`, described below.
- `"template"` — `{ template, purpose }`: one section of the bundled template (or its launcher, with `kind: "launcher"`) as verbatim bytes, and that section's one-line purpose from the published contract. The answer is the same whatever state the host's config is in. Use it as a worked example when writing that section for another backend.
- `"contract"` — `{ sections }`: every contract section in order, each with `marker`, `role` (`live` or `seed`) and `purpose`, and no section text.
- `"draft"` — a structural check of the draft config at `path`, with the same rules and fault vocabulary as the host config check, so a draft that passes is ready to swap in. Returns `{ outcome, instructions }`: `valid`; `invalid` with `fault` (`missing-sections` and its `sections`, or `malformed` and its `reason`); `absent` when no file is at `path`; `refused` when `path` is outside the project, and nothing is read. It checks structure, never content.

**Optional `kind` parameter** — host and template reads only: any section marker of the published brain contract (see the enum), live or seed; `"launcher"` only with `source: "template"`. Omitting it means `"orientation"`, the runtime briefing for reaching the brain mid-task. `"config"` is the integration's wiring flow that `/aide:brain config` runs. Seed sections are fetched one per call while seeding. `path` is required with `source: "draft"` and accepted nowhere else; any other combination is rejected before the tool runs.

**Host read response shape: exactly `{ status, instructions, found, purpose? }`.** No `backend`, no `connector`, no `name`, no `kind`.

- `found: true` — `instructions` is that section's verbatim bytes from the host's `.aide/config/brain.aide`: no trimming, no normalization, no `${...}` substitution. `purpose` is that section's one-line purpose from the published contract; use it when adapting the section for another backend.
- `found: false` — `instructions` is remediation, and `purpose` is absent. An absent file → run `/aide:brain config`. A requested section missing from the file → with the user's consent, call `aide_upgrade` with `category: "brain"`. A malformed or unreadable file → the exact fault, a hand fix with the user, then re-check with `aide_info`. Do not proceed as if the section were available.

The section is returned on every status where the config exists and is well-formed, including `brain-aide-invalid` with missing sections, `no-mcp-entry` and `mcp-drift`.

`status` mirrors the `BrainState` tagged union from `buildBrainState`, with five values: `ok`, `no-brain-aide`, `brain-aide-invalid`, `no-mcp-entry`, `mcp-drift`. Branch on `found` for "did I get the section" and on `status` for "is the brain healthy".

source.description: Which read runs. Omitted means `host`: one section of the host's `.aide/config/brain.aide`. `template`: one section or the launcher of the bundled template, with its purpose. `contract`: every contract section with its role and purpose. `draft`: a structural check of the draft config at `path`.

kind.description: Which section: any section marker of the published contract, live or seed, or `launcher` with `source: "template"` only. Omitted means `orientation`. Not accepted with `contract` or `draft`. Seed sections are fetched one per call while seeding.

path.description: Project-relative path of a draft brain config. Required with `source: "draft"` and accepted nowhere else; a path outside the project is refused unread.

tools.name: aide_init
tools.description:
Bootstrap the AIDE development environment into a project. Returns structured JSON for agent consumption — not prose.

The tool uses a two-call pattern for progressive disclosure:

**First call (no `category` param):** Returns a lightweight summary — every step with `name`, `status` (would-create/would-overwrite/would-skip/exists), `category`, and `filePath`, but NO `content` fields. Also returns `brainHints` (brain root candidates) and detected `framework`. Use this to understand what needs to be done and which categories require user prompts.

**Second call (with `category` param):** The tool writes all `would-create` AND approved `would-overwrite` files directly to disk itself and returns a manifest — steps with `filePath`, `status` (`created`, `overwritten`, or `exists`), and `name`, but NO `content`. `would-skip` steps stay `would-skip` in the manifest (tool writes nothing for them). The agent never sees file content and never uses the Write tool for new files.

**Exception — MCP steps:** For MCP steps, the manifest includes `prescription` data (key name and entry object) so the agent can read the existing config, merge, and write. The tool never touches MCP config directly.

**Exception — brain category:** The `Brain config (brain.aide)` step carries `brainSummary` on every call, including the summary: `sections` (each section's `marker`, `role`, `seedPath` for seeds, and `templateBytes`), `missingSections`, `staleSections`, `legacyLauncher` reasons and `templateIntegration`. It never carries section text, purposes, repair blocks or before/after bodies. Missing sections are inserted with `aide_upgrade` `category: "brain"`, seeds are read one at a time with `aide_brain`, and migrations are previewed and applied one at a time through `aide_upgrade`. Sections the user edited and custom launchers are never offered. The tool creates `.aide/config/brain.aide` when it is absent and never overwrites an existing one.

**Exception — session record:** The `Session record (session.aide)` step never carries content and the tool never writes it. When it is `would-create`, its `instructions` tell you to call `aide_scaffold` with directory "." and type "session" — do that, unprompted. When `.aide/session.aide` exists it is `exists` and is never overwritten.

**Exception — IDE VS Code steps:** IDE steps that need external tooling (VS Code CLI) return instructions for the agent to execute, since those aren't simple file writes.

**Agent branch logic — silent-on-create, prompt-on-overwrite:**

After the first call, walk the categories using this rule:
- **Pure-create category** (all steps are `would-create`, `would-skip`, or `exists`): apply silently by calling with `category=X` immediately — no AskUserQuestion. A category with nothing on disk to overwrite has no decision the user can inform.
- **Overwrite-bearing category** (any step is `would-overwrite`): pause and use AskUserQuestion with structured options. Name the files that would be overwritten. If the user approves, call with `category=X` — the tool overwrites and returns `overwritten` in the manifest. If the user declines an overwrite but wants the new files, call with `category=X` — the tool writes only `would-create` steps; the `would-overwrite` step stays `would-overwrite` in the manifest.
- **Inherent-decision categories** (framework, brain root path, MCP config merge, IDE choice): always use AskUserQuestion regardless of disk state. These are not file-write decisions — filesystem contents cannot resolve them.

**IMPORTANT — one-at-a-time wizard pattern using AskUserQuestion:**
Do NOT present a summary table of all categories. Do NOT offer "all" as an option. Do NOT ask conversational questions — use the `AskUserQuestion` tool with structured options at every pause point.

1. Call without `category` first to get the metadata
2. Present ONLY the detected framework — use AskUserQuestion with Yes/{alternatives} options. STOP.
3. Walk categories in order: methodology, commands, agents, skills, mcp, brain, ide, readme. For each:
   - Pure-create: apply silently (call with `category=X`), report results, move to next.
   - Overwrite-bearing: use AskUserQuestion naming the would-overwrite files. STOP. Wait for selection, then call with `category=X`. Report manifest (created N, overwrote M). Move to next.
   - Inherent decision: always use AskUserQuestion. STOP.
4. For brain: read `brainSummary` from the step, then direct the user to `/aide:brain config`. Call with `category=brain` only to receive the manifest; the tool creates `.aide/config/brain.aide` only when absent and never overwrites an existing one.
5. For MCP: when the aide step is would-create, its `globalPackage` names the aide server's global package. If `installed` is false, the step also carries `instructions`: act on them before merging — run its `installCommand` via Bash first — running AIDE's setup is the consent. If the install fails, tell the user plainly and stop: never merge an entry whose command is not installed. Then use AskUserQuestion with Merge/Skip and merge the `prescription` entry (the global `aidemd-mcp` command) into the existing config yourself (read → merge → write). Never replace an existing aide entry. STOP.
6. For IDE: use AskUserQuestion with multiSelect for Zed/VS Code/Neither. STOP.

Each pause point is ONE AskUserQuestion → wait for selection → then proceed. Never show multiple categories at once. Never ask open-ended conversational questions.

framework.description: Force a specific framework instead of auto-detecting. Use this when re-calling after the user confirms or overrides detection.

path.description: Custom project root path (defaults to server working directory)

category.description: Write all would-create and approved would-overwrite files for this category to disk and return a manifest (status: created/overwritten/exists; would-skip steps pass through unchanged). Omit on the first call to get a metadata-only summary of all steps.

tools.name: aide_inspect
tools.description: Return JSDoc, signature, and kind for a named symbol without opening the full file — Tier 2 progressive disclosure for code. When an agent knows a function name from an import list or orchestrator file, call inspect to learn what the symbol does, what it accepts, and what it returns, based on its contract alone. Searches across TypeScript and JavaScript source files (ts, tsx, js, jsx, mjs, cjs). Use the optional `file` parameter to narrow the search to a single file when the location is already known.

file.description: Optional file path to narrow search to a single file
